parentIntro: Equal groups → multiplication. The diagnostic says this is her comfort zone, so this week leans into the WHY: arrays show that 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 are the same thing seen sideways, and missing-value questions (“? groups of 5 make 30”) plant the seed of division. Expect depth days — let the app stretch her.
watchFor: The classic slip is adding instead of grouping — “3 groups of 4” answered as 7. If it appears, draw the groups. Also encourage skip-counting OUT LOUD (4, 8, 12…) — hearing the rhythm is how the times tables eventually stick with the why attached.

demo.title: Groups, arrays and the sideways trick
demo.say: Today is about counting things in groups — and a magic trick where turning a picture sideways gives you a second fact for free.

steps.caption: 3 groups of 4 apples
steps.say: Three groups of four apples. Let's skip count them: four, eight, twelve!

steps.caption: adding the same number again and again
steps.say: That's four plus four plus four. Adding the same number over and over — that's what multiplying is.

steps.caption: an array: 3 rows of 4
steps.say: Now line them up neatly. Three rows of four. This tidy rectangle is called an array.

steps.caption: turn it sideways — same answer!
steps.say: Here's the magic. Tip your head sideways — now it's four rows of three! Three times four and four times three are the same twelve. Every fact you learn gives you its twin for free.

weDo.problem: Draw an array for 5 rows of 3. Then find its sideways twin.
weDo.model: Dots on the whiteboard — neat rows matter, so the rectangle shape is visible. Count row by row, skip-counting aloud.
steps: She draws 5 rows of 3 dots. Skip count together: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
Ask: “Without drawing anything new — what's 3 × 5?” Let her tip her head at the same picture.
Write 3 × 5 = 15 next to it. Ask why the answer didn't change.

weDo.model: Skip count on fingers: every finger is one group of 5. Stop when you hit 30, count the fingers up.
steps: Read it together and ask what's missing (how many GROUPS, not how many in a group).
Skip count by 5 on fingers: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 — six fingers.
Sneaky follow-up if she's flying: “30 lollies shared into bags of 5 — how many bags?” (Same question wearing a disguise — that's division knocking.)
